Field studies of the Striped searobin (Prionotus evolans) indicate that females reach a maximum adult body mass of 584 grams [Wwi = 584 grams], a figure derived from length-weight relationships among mature individuals collected from continental shelf waters. The corresponding asymptotic total length for these large females is 45 centimeters [Li = 45 centimeters], representing the upper limit of somatic growth for this species. In contrast to these maximal values, the wet weight at birth is remarkably low at 0.0008 grams [Wwb = 0.0008 grams], reflecting the small size of the fertilized eggs, which have a diameter ranging from 1.05 to 1.25 millimeters. This enormous disparity between initial and ultimate mass emphasizes the rapid growth trajectory that characterizes the early life stages of this benthic predator. The yolksac larvae emerge following a relatively short incubation period.

Reproductive development in the Striped searobin is marked by a distinct size threshold at the onset of puberty. Extensive trawl surveys have established that the total length at puberty is 22.1 centimeters [Lp = 22.1 centimeters], a measurement that corresponds closely with the wet weight at puberty of 71.7 grams [Wwp = 71.7 grams] when evaluated using the species-specific length-mass conversion formula. Reaching this size typically occurs during the second year of life for individuals in the Mid-Atlantic Bight, though local variation in prey availability can shift this schedule by several months. The onset of gonadal maturation at these dimensions ensures that females have accumulated sufficient somatic reserves to support the energetic demands of vitellogenesis and subsequent spawning activity over the protracted breeding season.

Under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable water temperature of 12.7 °C [T = 12.7 °C], embryogenesis proceeds rapidly, with hatching occurring after only 8 days [ab = 8 days]. This abbreviated developmental duration is consistent with the pelagic egg strategy observed in many triglid fishes, where rapid eclosion minimizes the window of vulnerability to egg predators and physical dispersal from suitable nursery habitats. The newly emerged prolarvae measure approximately 3 to 4 millimeters in total length and rely entirely on their endogenous yolk reserves during the first several days post-hatching. The progression from yolk-sac larva to the onset of exogenous feeding is tightly coupled to the ambient thermal regime, with the 12.7 °C treatment producing consistent rates of yolk absorption and mouth gape development across replicate rearing trials.

Longevity records for the Striped searobin, derived from otolith aging of specimens collected across its geographic range, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 7 years [am = approximately 7 years] when maintained at a temperature of 12.7 °C [T = 12.7 °C]. This lifespan is moderate among North Atlantic triglids, falling between the shorter-lived northern searobin and the more extended longevities reported for certain Gulf of Mexico congeners. Comparative growth analysis between the sexes reveals that females attain a considerably larger adult body size than males, a pattern common among scorpionfishes where fecundity selection favors larger female body dimensions. The asymptotic mass of 584 grams [Wwi = 584 grams] in females contrasts sharply with the typical mass of mature males, and the corresponding structural length of 45 centimeters [Li = 45 centimeters] places females at the upper end of the species' size spectrum. Gonadal maturation in females is initiated at a total length of 22.1 centimeters [Lp = 22.1 centimeters], at which point the ovaries commence vitellogenic activity and the individual attains a wet weight at puberty of 71.7 grams [Wwp = 71.7 grams]. These size-based reproductive thresholds ensure that first spawning occurs only after sufficient structural growth has been completed, an adaptation that buffers against reproductive failure in years of poor foraging conditions on the continental shelf.
